```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
set.seed(1)
```

Two power meters on the same bike rarely agree exactly, and the interesting
question is not whether they differ but by how much, and whether the gap is
steady or opens up as you push harder. This vignette walks through that
comparison, then through the harder case where a third meter has to be brought
onto the same scale without ever having been ridden alongside the first.

```{r setup}
library(cyclingpower)
```

Everything below runs on `demo_rides()`, which writes a small set of ride files
with distortions chosen in advance, so every number has a known answer to check
against. Two sessions:

| Run | Meters | What was planted |
|---|---|---|
| run1 | assioma, kickr | kickr reads 2.5% low, and its clock runs 7 s fast |
| run2 | assioma, quarq | quarq reads 3% low below 200 W and 5% high above it |

assioma is in both, which is what makes the third meter reachable at the end.

```{r demo}
dir <- demo_rides()
list.files(dir)
```

Real files replace these unchanged. `vignette("recording_rides")` covers how to
record them, and several of the decisions there — recording rate, auto-pause,
and what to actually ride — determine whether the steps below can work at all.

## Getting files into the comparison

The unit of analysis is a run, meaning one session ridden once, recorded by two
or more sources. Hand `read_rides()` a directory and it reads the `run` and
`source` labels off filenames shaped `run1_kickr.csv`:

```{r read}
rides <- read_rides(dir)
rides
```

Every reader returns this same shape whatever the file format, so a GPX
exported from Strava and a FIT pulled off a head unit arrive with the same
column names and types. `time` and `power` are always present; the other
channels appear when the file carries them.

Where the filenames do not carry the labels, build the table yourself and pass
that instead — `read_rides()` takes a data frame of `path`, `run` and `source`
just as happily as a directory. A filename that does not split cleanly is an
error rather than a silently missing label.

```{r read-file}
one <- read_file(file.path(dir, "run1_kickr.csv"))
head(one, 3)
```

## Putting the sources on one clock

That seven-second offset matters more than it looks. Differencing the two
series on their nominal timestamps compares power from one moment against power
from another, which inflates the spread and shifts the average difference, and
nothing about the result announces that it has happened. `align_rides()`
resamples each source onto a one-second grid and recovers the offset by
cross-correlating the power traces.

```{r align}
aligned <- align_rides(rides)
alignment_report(aligned)
```

The seven seconds planted in kickr's clock come back as seven. The report is
worth reading rather than skipping: `offset` is the correction applied,
`correlation` how well the traces matched at that offset, and `status` whether
the offset was established at all. Where both channels came off a single head
unit the offset is simply zero and the same code path serves. Where a ride was
too steady to lock onto — a long block at constant power has no features to
align against — the status comes back `unresolved`, the recorded timestamps
stand, and a warning says so.

```{r timeseries}
plot_timeseries(aligned)
```

## How far apart do they read?

```{r agreement}
power_agreement(aligned)
```

The sentence above the table is the answer; the columns are there to check it.
`bias_w` is the average difference in watts and `gain_pc` the same thing
multiplicatively, which is usually the more natural way to think about a power
meter, since meters tend to be a few per cent out rather than a fixed number of
watts out. kickr was built to read 2.5 per cent low, and assioma against it
comes back at about 2.6 per cent, which is `1 / 0.975 - 1`. `loa_lo` and
`loa_hi` bound the range within which most individual seconds fall — a much
wider range than the interval on the average, and a different question.

Look at run2, though. Its interval straddles zero, which reads as *these two
meters agree*. Hold that thought.

The intervals come from a moving-block bootstrap rather than from treating each
second as an independent observation. Per-second power is heavily
autocorrelated — what you are riding now is nearly what you were riding a second
ago — so an hour's recording carries far less independent information than its
3,600 rows suggest, and an interval built on the independence assumption would
be roughly an order of magnitude too narrow.

```{r bland-altman}
plot_agreement(aligned)
```

## Does the gap change with effort?

A single average difference hides the pattern that usually matters, which is a
meter agreeing at endurance pace and drifting at threshold.
`agreement_by_level()` bins the seconds by the mean of the two readings and
reports the difference within each band.

```{r by-level}
by_level <- agreement_by_level(aligned, width = 25)
plot_by_level(by_level, scale = "percent")
```

There is run2. The overall figure said the two meters agreed to within half a
per cent; the bands show quarq reading about three per cent low up to 200 W and
about five per cent high above it. The average was not wrong — the errors really
do cancel over this ride — but it describes no part of the range, and on a ride
weighted differently it would have come out somewhere else entirely.

Binning on the mean rather than on one nominated meter is deliberate. If you bin
by assioma and then plot assioma minus quarq against those bins, assioma's own
measurement noise pushes the points into a slope, and you see a trend that is an
artefact of the plotting rather than a property of the meters.

`level_dependence()` states it rather than leaving it to the eye:

```{r level-dependence}
level_dependence(by_level)
```

`separated` is whether the extreme bands' 95% intervals overlap, so a pair with
too few seconds to resolve anything simply does not fire. run1's clean 2.5 per
cent gain is flat across the range and does not separate; run2 does.

`seconds` travels with every row because time is not spread evenly across the
power range. The ends are usually thin, and an estimate resting on twenty
seconds deserves less weight than one resting on six hundred.

## Bringing in a third meter

Now the awkward case. run1 carried assioma and kickr, run2 carried assioma and
quarq. kickr and quarq have never been on the bike together, so there is no
second at which both were measuring. assioma is the bridge: each run gives a
gain relative to it, and the difference between those two gains is kickr
against quarq.

```{r chain}
chained <- chain_sources(aligned)
chained
```

The `basis` column marks the last row as chained rather than directly observed,
and that distinction is the point: the two direct comparisons rest on seconds
where both meters measured the same effort, while the chained one rests on an
assumption as well.

```{r chain-plot}
plot_chain(chained)
```

The assumption is that assioma read the same on both days, and nothing in the
ride files can test it. A meter that drifted between the two sessions moves the
kickr-to-quarq figure by exactly the amount it drifted, and the data offer no
way to tell that apart from a genuine difference between the two. That is why
the print method says so without being asked. `chain_report()` states it again
and reports what *can* be checked, which is whether the two runs covered
comparable power — gains estimated over different parts of the range are not
really comparable at all.

```{r chain-report}
report <- chain_report(chained)
report$assumption
report$overlap
report$coverage
```

Note also that the chained interval is wider than either direct one it is built
from. It has to be: two independently bootstrapped runs are being subtracted.

## Doing all of it at once

`compare_report()` runs this whole sequence and writes it out as a single HTML
document, which is usually what you want once the exploration is done. It takes
the same directory:

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
compare_report(dir, "power-comparison.html")
```

`launch_app()` opens the same pipeline as a local web interface, with the
settings live and a download button that renders the report from the results
already on screen.

## Reading FIT files

FIT needs [FITfileR](https://github.com/grimbough/FITfileR), which is not on
CRAN. Everything above works without it; only `.fit` input needs it.

```{r fit, eval = requireNamespace("FITfileR", quietly = TRUE)}
read_file(system.file("extdata", "power1.fit", package = "cyclingpower")) |>
  head(3)
```
